### 2. 🪟 Property Injection (The Dead Drop)
The supplies show up *after* the object is created, left at a designated spot.

```csharp
public class MobBoss
{
    public IGetawayDriver Driver { get; set; } // Set it from outside
    
    public void PullHeist() => Driver.Drive();
}
```

## 🏦 The DI Container (Your Crime Syndicate's Logistics Operation)

Running this all manually is small-time. Real bosses let **the Organization** (the DI Container) handle all the logistics.

citations.cited_text: The framework takes on the responsibility of creating an instance of the dependency and disposing of it when it's no longer needed.
citations.title: Dependency injection - .NET | Microsoft Learn

content.text: The framework takes on the responsibility of creating an instance of the dependency and disposing of it when it's no longer needed.

You register your crew in `Program.cs` like putting people on the payroll:

```csharp
// Register your crew
services.AddTransient<IGetawayDriver, CarDriver>();
```

And then the DI Container automatically hands the right driver to the boss — no questions asked.

## ⏳ Service Lifetimes (How Long Your Crew Sticks Around)

citations.cited_text: When registering services, you can specify their lifetimes: Transient: A new instance is provided every time the service is requested. Scoped: A singl...
citations.title: Mastering Dependency Injection in C# and .NET Core: A Comprehensive Guide with Code Examples - DEV Community

content.text:
When registering services, you can specify their lifetimes:
- **Transient**: A new instance is provided *every time* the service is requested.
- **Scoped**: A single instance is provided *per request*.
- **Singleton**: A single instance is created and *shared throughout the application's lifetime*.

```csharp
services.AddTransient<IGetawayDriver, CarDriver>();   // New driver every job
services.AddScoped<IGetawayDriver, CarDriver>();      // Same driver per mission
services.AddSingleton<IGetawayDriver, CarDriver>();   // ONE driver for life
```

content.text: By using the DI pattern, your class doesn't depend on a concrete type — only the **interface** it implements. This design makes it easy to change the implementation without modifying the class itself.
